title: Logistics Warehouse Office Scope Tasks: High-Touch & Floor Maintenance Routines for Front Office & Dispatch
seoTitle: Logistics Warehouse Office Scope Tasks: Dispatch Cleaning Checklist
metaDescription: Logistics warehouse office scope tasks by day, week, and month, with labor minutes that push dispatch bids above 3,500 sq ft/hr. Compare quotes in our tool.
excerpt: This checklist breaks a warehouse front office and dispatch scope into nightly, weekly, monthly, and quarterly tasks with realistic labor minutes. It also flags the specialty items, from dock-entry grit control to driver restroom resets, that pull production below standard office rates and raise the bid.
quickAnswer: A warehouse front office scope should list nightly trash, restroom, high-touch, and dispatch-lane floor tasks; weekly detail dusting and full damp mopping; monthly vent, baseboard, and partition work; and quarterly scrub-and-recoat of VCT. Specialty tasks such as dock-entry grit removal and driver restroom resets typically slow effective production by 15 to 30 percent versus the 3,500 sq ft per hour office benchmark, adding 20 to 45 minutes per visit at $35 to $65 per labor hour.

blocks.text: Why a generic office checklist fails at the dispatch counter

Most janitorial scopes are written for carpeted professional suites: empty trash, vacuum, wipe desks, clean restrooms. Drop that template into a distribution center front office and the gaps show up within two weeks. Grit from the dock drifts 30 feet into the office, the driver restroom runs out of towels by noon, the dispatch window glass is covered in handprints, and the break table is sticky from three shifts of vending machine snacks. None of those problems are exotic. They are simply not on the list, so the crew does not do them and the vendor does not price them.

A good scope of work for a warehouse office is written by zone and frequency, with an estimated minute value for each task. That structure lets you see exactly where labor goes, hold the night crew to a verifiable standard, and understand why a dispatch office bid can legitimately run 20 to 40 percent above a standard office of the same square footage.

blocks.caption: Nightly scope for a 4,000 sq ft warehouse front office with three restrooms (minutes per visit)
rows: Shake or vacuum walk-off mats, dust mop grit lane, damp mop with neutral cleaner, wipe door push plates
Clean pass-through glass both sides, disinfect counter, pens, sign-in tablet bezels, empty trash
Empty trash and recycling, spot-clean desks, vacuum or dust mop, wipe phones and door handles
Clean and disinfect fixtures, refill paper and soap, mop floors, check urinal screens
Wipe tables, counters, microwave, sink; empty trash; mop floor
Standard office of same size and restroom count: about 100 - 110 minutes

blocks.text: At the 3,500 sq ft per hour production benchmark, 4,000 sq ft of open office should take about 69 minutes, plus roughly 9 to 12 minutes per standard restroom and a few minutes for a light-use breakroom, or about 100 to 110 minutes in total. The table above lands at 123 to 155 minutes because the dock vestibule and dispatch counter behave like a retail entrance rather than an office corridor, and the driver restroom needs a full reset. At standard labor rates of $35 to $65 per hour, those extra 20 to 45 minutes add about $12 to $49 per visit, or roughly $150 to $635 a month at three visits a week.

items: Weekly: full damp mop of every hard floor, not just traffic lanes, using a dual-compartment bucket like the Unger 15-gallon SmartColor system so rinse water does not re-soil the VCT.
Weekly: high and low dusting of window ledges facing the yard, dispatch monitors, label printers, and the tops of filing cabinets where diesel soot settles.
Weekly: detail clean of breakroom appliances, including refrigerator door gaskets and vending machine fronts.
Monthly: vacuum HVAC return grilles and wipe supply diffusers; dock-side offices pull dust faster than interior suites.
Monthly: scrub baseboards and the lower 12 inches of walls along the dock entry lane where pallet-jack wheels and boots leave scuffs.
Monthly: clean interior glass partitions and both sides of the dispatch window frame and track.
Quarterly: machine scrub and recoat VCT in the office, with a full strip and five-coat refinish of the dock-entry lane two to four times a year depending on driver volume.
Quarterly: hot-water extraction of any carpeted private offices or conference rooms.

blocks.title: Put the dust mop before the wet mop
blocks.text: A 36-inch cotton dust mop on a 360-degree swivel frame, such as the Rubbermaid Commercial lobby frame with its 60-inch handle, can sweep a 40-foot dispatch corridor in a few passes. Dry-removing grit first keeps it from turning into slurry in the mop bucket and scratching the finish, which protects the floor program you are already paying for.
Which tasks push labor hours above standard office rates

Vendors build bids from production rates, so any task that slows square-foot coverage raises price. In a dispatch office, five items do most of the damage. First, grit and moisture control at the dock entry requires dry and wet passes plus mat maintenance every night. Second, driver restrooms need a full reset rather than a touch-up because of splash load and paper overuse. Third, glass and counters at the driver window need both-side cleaning and disinfection. Fourth, live operations: if dispatch runs a second or third shift, the crew must work around occupied desks, which can cut production by a quarter. Fifth, any engineered wood or LVT in a customer-facing lobby needs a low-moisture method, such as an 18-inch microfiber flat mop system with wood-safe solution, which is slower than a string mop.

Specialty work like strip-and-recoat or carpet extraction is usually priced at specialty rates of $55 to $95 per hour or amortized at $0.03 to $0.06 per sq ft per month. Keep it as a separate line so you can compare vendors on routine work and periodic work independently.
Writing exclusions so nothing falls through the cracks

items.name: Draw the boundary
items.text: Mark the office envelope on a floor plan and state that warehouse racking aisles, dock plates, and forklift charging areas are excluded unless separately priced.

items.name: Assign the locker room
items.text: Decide whether warehouse locker rooms and their restrooms belong to the office vendor or the industrial cleaning contractor, and write it down.

items.name: Define consumables ownership
items.text: State whether the vendor or your facilities team buys towels, tissue, soap, and liners, and who monitors par levels in the driver restroom.

items.name: Set inspection points
items.text: Use a monthly walk with a scored checklist covering the dock vestibule, dispatch window, and driver restroom, the three areas most likely to generate complaints.

blocks.text: Turning the checklist into a bid you can compare

Send every bidder the same zone table with minute estimates and frequencies, and ask them to confirm or adjust each line. A bidder who cuts dock-entry time to five minutes is telling you how they plan to win on price. A bidder who adds a mid-shift restroom check for the driver room may be more expensive but is pricing the real workload. Once the scope is standardized, compare per-visit totals and implied hourly rates rather than headline monthly numbers.

faqs.q: How many minutes should a cleaner spend on a warehouse dispatch office each night?
faqs.a: For a 4,000 sq ft office with three restrooms and a breakroom, plan on 123 to 155 minutes of labor per visit. That compares with roughly 100 to 110 minutes for a standard carpeted office of the same size once restrooms are included, with the difference coming almost entirely from the dock entry, dispatch window, and driver restroom.

faqs.q: Should restroom supplies be part of the cleaning scope?
faqs.a: It depends on who wants control of cost. Vendor-supplied consumables usually add $0.012 to $0.025 per sq ft per visit and shift restock risk to the vendor. If you buy them yourself, specify controlled dispensers and require the crew to log par levels so driver restrooms do not run out between visits.

faqs.q: How often does VCT in a warehouse office need to be stripped?
faqs.a: The dock-entry lane often needs a full strip and refinish every three to six months, while the rest of the office can usually be scrubbed and recoated quarterly and stripped once a year. Budget $0.03 to $0.06 per sq ft per month amortized and write the dates into the contract.

faqs.q: What safety documentation should a dispatch office cleaner carry?
faqs.a: The vendor should maintain Safety Data Sheets for every product under OSHA HazCom (29 CFR 1910.1200), train crew on container labeling, and provide a bloodborne pathogens exposure plan if they clean first-aid areas or bodily fluid spills. Many distribution centers also require site safety orientation and high-visibility vests whenever crew members cross dock or yard areas.

faqs.q: Is a Green Seal certified product program worth requiring?
faqs.a: For most dispatch offices, requiring Green Seal GS-37 or UL ECOLOGO certified general-purpose and restroom cleaners costs little or nothing extra and reduces fragrance and irritant complaints in small, poorly ventilated driver areas. Keep a registered disinfectant for restroom touch points, since green cleaners alone do not carry disinfection claims.
